Validation against other simulators

Source: vignettes/validation.Rmd
validation.Rmd
library(simpexp)

A simulator is only useful if one can trust what it produces. This vignette checks simpexp in the strongest form available: the same data-generating process is implemented in simpexp and in another, independent package, the same model is fitted to both samples, and the estimates are compared with each other and – wherever it exists – with the closed-form truth.

Where a closed form exists it is the reference, not the other simulator. Two simulators agreeing with each other is weaker evidence than both agreeing with an exact calculation.

1. Single event: msm::rpexp

msm::rpexp() draws piecewise exponential times by exactly the same inversion argument, and is an independent implementation of it. The difference is interface rather than method: it takes one rate vector per call, so with covariates it has to be called once per subject.

library(msm); library(survival)

cut   <- c(0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 10)
lrate <- c(-2.2, -1.8, -1.5, -1.9, -2.4, -2.0, -1.7)   # log baseline per interval
beta  <- 0.6
n     <- 4000

sim_simpexp <- function(dat)
  sim_pexp(~ lrate[interval] + beta * x, dat, cut = cut)

sim_rpexp <- function(dat) {
  tt <- vapply(dat$x, function(xi) {
    r <- exp(lrate + beta * xi)
    msm::rpexp(1, c(r, r[length(r)]), cut)
  }, 0)
  data.frame(id = dat$id, x = dat$x, tstop = pmin(tt, 10),
    status = as.integer(tt <= 10))
}

B <- 10
est <- vapply(seq_len(B), function(b) {
  set.seed(1000 + b)
  dat <- data.frame(id = 1:n, x = rbinom(n, 1, 0.5))
  c(simpexp = coef(coxph(Surv(tstop, status) ~ x, sim_simpexp(dat))),
    rpexp   = coef(coxph(Surv(tstop, status) ~ x, sim_rpexp(dat))))
}, numeric(2))

data.frame(
  source   = c("simpexp", "msm::rpexp"),
  estimate = rowMeans(est),
  mc_se    = apply(est, 1, sd) / sqrt(B),
  truth    = beta,
  row.names = NULL)
#>       source  estimate      mc_se truth
#> 1    simpexp 0.6235827 0.01065173   0.6
#> 2 msm::rpexp 0.5870984 0.01160832   0.6

Both recover the log hazard ratio, and the Monte-Carlo standard errors show that the remaining difference is noise. The two samples are also distributionally indistinguishable:

set.seed(42)
dat <- data.frame(id = 1:20000, x = rbinom(20000, 1, 0.5))
a <- sim_simpexp(dat); b <- sim_rpexp(dat)
suppressWarnings(ks.test(a$tstop, b$tstop))
#> 
#>  Asymptotic two-sample Kolmogorov-Smirnov test
#> 
#> data:  a$tstop and b$tstop
#> D = 0.00705, p-value = 0.7029
#> alternative hypothesis: two-sided

The price of the per-subject interface is speed. For 100 000 subjects on this grid, rpexp() called once per subject takes about 650 ms, against about 8 ms for the vectorised draw inside simpexp – same algorithm, same output, two orders of magnitude apart, because the loop pays R’s call overhead per subject.

2. A continuous hazard: simsurv

simpexp approximates a continuous hazard by a step function; simsurv inverts the continuous cumulative hazard itself. The discretisation is then the only difference between them, and it is instructive to watch it vanish as the grid is refined. The data-generating process is Weibull, h(t)=λγtγ−1eβxh(t) = \lambda\gamma t^{\gamma-1}e^{\beta x}, and the fitted model is a Weibull regression – the correct parametric model for the continuous version, and hence a model that should expose any discretisation bias.

library(simsurv)

lambda <- 0.08; gamma <- 1.4; beta_x <- -0.5
n <- 5000
log_h <- function(t, x) log(lambda * gamma) + (gamma - 1) * log(t) + beta_x * x

weib_fit <- function(time, status, x) {
  m  <- survreg(Surv(time, status) ~ x, dist = "weibull")
  sh <- 1 / m$scale
  c(shape = sh, lambda = exp(-sh * coef(m)[["(Intercept)"]]),
    beta = -coef(m)[["x"]] * sh, se_beta = sh * sqrt(vcov(m)["x", "x"]))
}

set.seed(7)
dat <- data.frame(id = 1:n, x = rnorm(n))
ss  <- simsurv(dist = "weibull", lambdas = lambda, gammas = gamma,
               betas = c(x = beta_x), x = dat, maxt = 10)
ss  <- merge(ss, dat, by = "id")

rows <- list(truth   = c(shape = gamma, lambda = lambda, beta = beta_x, se_beta = NA),
             simsurv = weib_fit(ss$eventtime, ss$status, ss$x))
for (by in c(1, 0.25, 0.05)) {
  sp <- sim_pexp(~ log_h(t, x), dat, cut = seq(0, 10, by = by))
  rows[[paste0("simpexp, by = ", by)]] <- weib_fit(sp$tstop, sp$status, sp$x)
}
round(do.call(rbind, rows), 4)
#>                     shape lambda    beta se_beta
#> truth              1.4000 0.0800 -0.5000      NA
#> simsurv            1.3930 0.0824 -0.4772  0.0162
#> simpexp, by = 1    1.2582 0.1166 -0.4597  0.0161
#> simpexp, by = 0.25 1.3487 0.0905 -0.5039  0.0163
#> simpexp, by = 0.05 1.3898 0.0835 -0.4914  0.0162

The shape parameter is the quantity the grid costs: a step function cannot reproduce a power-law hazard on coarse intervals, and the fitted shape is pulled towards 1. Refining the grid removes it. The covariate effect, in contrast, moves only within its own standard error (se_beta) – discretising the baseline does not bias the proportional effect, which is the usual reason a coarse grid is tolerable in practice.

Averaged over replications, the two simulators agree with the truth and with each other:

B <- 10; n <- 4000
cuts <- seq(0, 10, by = 0.02)
est <- vapply(seq_len(B), function(b) {
  set.seed(2000 + b)
  dat <- data.frame(id = 1:n, x = rnorm(n))
  ss  <- simsurv(dist = "weibull", lambdas = lambda, gammas = gamma,
                 betas = c(x = beta_x), x = dat, maxt = 10)
  ss  <- merge(ss, dat, by = "id")
  sp  <- sim_pexp(~ log_h(t, x), dat, cut = cuts)
  c(simsurv = coef(coxph(Surv(eventtime, status) ~ x, ss)),
    simpexp = coef(coxph(Surv(tstop, status) ~ x, sp)))
}, numeric(2))
data.frame(source = c("simsurv", "simpexp"), estimate = rowMeans(est),
  mc_se = apply(est, 1, sd) / sqrt(B), truth = beta_x, row.names = NULL)
#>    source   estimate       mc_se truth
#> 1 simsurv -0.4987259 0.005103460  -0.5
#> 2 simpexp -0.5056871 0.005156509  -0.5

3. Competing risks: latent failure times, and the closed form

For competing risks there are two textbook constructions. One draws a latent failure time per cause from the cause-specific hazard and keeps the minimum; the other – the one simpexp uses – draws the waiting time from the all-cause hazard and then the cause with probabilities hj(t)/∑khk(t)h_j(t)/\sum_k h_k(t). Under independent latent times the two give the same cause-specific hazards, so they must produce the same data.

With piecewise constant hazards, the exact probabilities are available, so all of this can be checked against a calculation rather than against another sample. For a subject with covariate xx:

P(cause j)=∑intervals lhjl∑khkl(e−H(κl−1)−e−H(κl)),P(\text{cause } j) \;=\; \sum_{\text{intervals } l} \frac{h_{jl}}{\sum_k h_{kl}} \Bigl( e^{-H(\kappa_{l-1})} - e^{-H(\kappa_l)} \Bigr),

with HH the all-cause cumulative hazard.

cut   <- c(0, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 12)
r_rel <- c(0.10, 0.22, 0.18, 0.12, 0.08, 0.05)
r_dth <- c(0.04, 0.05, 0.06, 0.08, 0.10, 0.12)
b_rel <- 0.5; b_dth <- -0.3
dt    <- diff(cut)

n <- 50000
set.seed(7); dat <- data.frame(id = 1:n, x = rnorm(n))

# exact probabilities, for this very covariate vector
exact <- rowMeans(vapply(dat$x, function(xi) {
  a <- r_rel * exp(b_rel * xi); b <- r_dth * exp(b_dth * xi)
  ra <- a + b; H <- c(0, cumsum(ra * dt))
  p  <- exp(-head(H, -1)) - exp(-H[-1])
  c(cens = exp(-H[length(H)]), relapse = sum(a / ra * p), death = sum(b / ra * p))
}, numeric(3)))

# simpexp: all-cause hazard, then the cause
sp <- sim_pexp_cr(list(relapse = ~ log(r_rel[interval]) + b_rel * x,
                       death   = ~ log(r_dth[interval]) + b_dth * x),
                  dat, cut = cut)
sp_share <- prop.table(table(ifelse(sp$status == 0L, "cens", as.character(sp$to))))

# latent failure times: one piecewise exponential time per cause, minimum wins
one <- function(rates, bb) vapply(dat$x, function(xi)
  msm::rpexp(1, c(rates, rates[length(rates)]) * exp(bb * xi), cut), 0)
t1 <- one(r_rel, b_rel); t2 <- one(r_dth, b_dth)
tt <- pmin(t1, t2, 12)
lat_share <- prop.table(table(
  ifelse(tt == 12, "cens", ifelse(t1 < t2, "relapse", "death"))))

round(rbind(exact = exact,
            simpexp = sp_share[names(exact)],
            latent  = lat_share[names(exact)]), 4)
#>           cens relapse  death
#> exact   0.0900  0.5659 0.3441
#> simpexp 0.0881  0.5643 0.3475
#> latent  0.0899  0.5650 0.3452

All three agree to within the Monte-Carlo error of a share at this sample size (about 0.0022). The same holds for the cause-specific regression coefficients, fitted with one and the same model to both samples:

cs_cox <- function(time, cause, x)
  c(relapse = coef(coxph(Surv(time, cause == "relapse") ~ x)),
    death   = coef(coxph(Surv(time, cause == "death") ~ x)))

B <- 10; n <- 3000
est <- lapply(seq_len(B), function(b) {
  set.seed(500 + b)
  dat <- data.frame(id = 1:n, x = rnorm(n))
  sp <- sim_pexp_cr(list(relapse = ~ log(r_rel[interval]) + b_rel * x,
                         death   = ~ log(r_dth[interval]) + b_dth * x),
                    dat, cut = cut)
  one <- function(rates, bb) vapply(dat$x, function(xi)
    msm::rpexp(1, c(rates, rates[length(rates)]) * exp(bb * xi), cut), 0)
  t1 <- one(r_rel, b_rel); t2 <- one(r_dth, b_dth); tt <- pmin(t1, t2, 12)
  rbind(
    simpexp = cs_cox(sp$tstop, ifelse(sp$status == 0L, "cens", as.character(sp$to)), sp$x),
    latent  = cs_cox(tt, ifelse(tt == 12, "cens", ifelse(t1 < t2, "relapse", "death")), dat$x))
})
arr <- simplify2array(est)                     # simulator x coefficient x rep
m   <- apply(arr, 1:2, mean)
se  <- apply(arr, 1:2, sd) / sqrt(B)
colnames(m) <- colnames(se) <- c("relapse", "death")
round(rbind(truth = c(relapse = b_rel, death = b_dth), m,
            `mc se (simpexp)` = se["simpexp", ],
            `mc se (latent)`  = se["latent", ]), 4)
#>                 relapse   death
#> truth            0.5000 -0.3000
#> simpexp          0.4970 -0.3086
#> latent           0.4827 -0.2890
#> mc se (simpexp)  0.0048  0.0091
#> mc se (latent)   0.0112  0.0095

4. Multi-state, Markov: msm::sim.msm and a fitted msm model

Here the comparison can be made in the most direct way imaginable: simulate a time-homogeneous illness-death process with recovery, once with msm::sim.msm() and once with simpexp, then fit the same msm model with exact transition times to both data sets and compare the estimated intensity matrices.

q <- rbind(c(0, 0.35, 0.05), c(0.50, 0, 0.12), c(0, 0, 0))
states <- c("healthy", "ill", "dead")
dimnames(q) <- list(states, states)
maxt <- 10; n <- 1500
set.seed(11)

panel_from_msm <- function(n) {
  d <- do.call(rbind, lapply(seq_len(n), function(i) {
    s <- msm::sim.msm(q, maxtime = maxt)
    data.frame(id = i, time = s$times, state = s$states)
  }))
  d
}

panel_from_simpexp <- function(n) {
  s <- sim_pexp_msm(list(
    transition("healthy", "ill",     ~ log(0.35)),
    transition("healthy", "dead",    ~ log(0.05)),
    transition("ill",     "healthy", ~ log(0.50)),
    transition("ill",     "dead",    ~ log(0.12))),
    data.frame(id = seq_len(n)), cut = c(0, maxt))
  first <- s[s$episode == 1L, c("id", "tstart", "from")]
  moved <- s[s$status == 1L,  c("id", "tstop", "to")]
  stuck <- s[s$status == 0L,  c("id", "tstop", "from")]   # censored: state unchanged
  names(first) <- names(moved) <- names(stuck) <- c("id", "time", "state")
  d <- rbind(first, moved, stuck)
  d$state <- match(as.character(d$state), states)
  d[order(d$id, d$time), ]
}

fit_msm <- function(d) {
  m <- msm::msm(state ~ time, subject = id, data = d, qmatrix = q,
                exacttimes = TRUE, control = list(fnscale = 4000))
  qq <- msm::qmatrix.msm(m, ci = "none")
  c(`healthy->ill` = qq[1, 2], `healthy->dead` = qq[1, 3],
    `ill->healthy` = qq[2, 1], `ill->dead` = qq[2, 3])
}

B <- 5
est <- lapply(seq_len(B), function(b) {
  set.seed(300 + b)
  rbind(`msm::sim.msm` = fit_msm(panel_from_msm(n)),
        simpexp        = fit_msm(panel_from_simpexp(n)))
})
arr <- simplify2array(est)
m   <- apply(arr, 1:2, mean); se <- apply(arr, 1:2, sd) / sqrt(B)
round(rbind(truth = c(0.35, 0.05, 0.50, 0.12), m,
            `mc se (msm)`     = se["msm::sim.msm", ],
            `mc se (simpexp)` = se["simpexp", ]), 4)
#>                 healthy->ill healthy->dead ill->healthy ill->dead
#> truth                 0.3500        0.0500       0.5000    0.1200
#> msm::sim.msm          0.3474        0.0497       0.5099    0.1235
#> simpexp               0.3548        0.0492       0.5038    0.1197
#> mc se (msm)           0.0020        0.0008       0.0084    0.0029
#> mc se (simpexp)       0.0034        0.0012       0.0034    0.0021

The transition counts match as well (one replication; the diagonal holds the censored observations, whose state is unchanged at their last observation time):

set.seed(301)
list(`msm::sim.msm` = msm::statetable.msm(state, id, panel_from_msm(n)),
     simpexp        = msm::statetable.msm(state, id, panel_from_simpexp(n)))
#> $`msm::sim.msm`
#>     to
#> from    1    2    3
#>    1  446 2519  364
#>    2 1829  273  417
#> 
#> $simpexp
#>     to
#> from    1    2    3
#>    1  428 2553  353
#>    2 1834  273  446

5. Multi-state, semi-Markov: gems

gems builds a multi-state process from latent transition times on the clock-reset scale: for each possible transition out of the current state it draws a sojourn time from a parametric distribution and takes the minimum. That makes it an independent check of the semi-Markov case. The process below is a progressive illness-death model – gems stores one entry time per state and therefore cannot represent recurrence, so recovery is left out here.

The sojourn time in ill before death is Weibull with shape 1.6, which in simpexp is written as the Weibull hazard in t_sojourn.

library(gems)
sh <- 1.6; sc <- 6; r_hi <- 0.35; r_hd <- 0.05
maxt <- 10; n <- 4000

run_gems <- function(n, seed) {
  set.seed(seed)
  hf <- generateHazardMatrix(3)
  hf[[1, 2]] <- "Exponential"; hf[[1, 3]] <- "Exponential"; hf[[2, 3]] <- "Weibull"
  pm <- generateParameterMatrix(hf)
  pm[[1, 2]] <- list(r_hi); pm[[1, 3]] <- list(r_hd); pm[[2, 3]] <- list(sh, sc)
  suppressMessages(
    g <- simulateCohort(transitionFunctions = hf, parameters = pm,
                        cohortSize = n, to = maxt))
  tt <- as.data.frame(g@time.to.state)
  data.frame(id = seq_len(n), t_ill = tt[[2]], t_dead = tt[[3]])
}

run_simpexp <- function(n, seed, by = 0.02) {
  set.seed(seed)
  s <- sim_pexp_msm(list(
    transition("healthy", "ill",  ~ log(r_hi)),
    transition("healthy", "dead", ~ log(r_hd)),
    transition("ill",     "dead", ~ log(sh / sc) + (sh - 1) * log(t_sojourn / sc))),
    data.frame(id = seq_len(n)), cut = seq(0, maxt, by = by))
  ill  <- s[s$from == "healthy" & !is.na(s$to) & s$to == "ill", ]
  dead <- s[!is.na(s$to) & s$to == "dead", ]
  data.frame(id = seq_len(n),
    t_ill  = ill$tstop[match(seq_len(n), ill$id)],
    t_dead = dead$tstop[match(seq_len(n), dead$id)])
}

One and the same analysis is applied to both: occurrence/exposure rates for the two exits out of healthy, and a Weibull model for the sojourn time in ill.

analyse <- function(d) {
  d$t_ill[!is.na(d$t_ill) & d$t_ill > maxt]     <- NA
  d$t_dead[!is.na(d$t_dead) & d$t_dead > maxt]  <- NA
  exit  <- pmin(ifelse(is.na(d$t_ill),  Inf, d$t_ill),
                ifelse(is.na(d$t_dead), Inf, d$t_dead), maxt)
  n_ill <- sum(!is.na(d$t_ill))
  n_dth <- sum(!is.na(d$t_dead) & (is.na(d$t_ill) | d$t_dead < d$t_ill))
  ill   <- d[!is.na(d$t_ill), ]
  soj   <- pmin(ifelse(is.na(ill$t_dead), maxt, ill$t_dead), maxt) - ill$t_ill
  ev    <- as.integer(!is.na(ill$t_dead) & ill$t_dead <= maxt)
  k     <- soj > 0
  m     <- survreg(Surv(soj[k], ev[k]) ~ 1, dist = "weibull")
  c(`healthy->ill` = n_ill / sum(exit), `healthy->dead` = n_dth / sum(exit),
    `sojourn shape` = 1 / m$scale,
    `sojourn scale` = exp(coef(m)[["(Intercept)"]]))
}

B <- 10
G <- vapply(seq_len(B), function(b) analyse(run_gems(n, 100 + b)), numeric(4))
S <- vapply(seq_len(B), function(b) analyse(run_simpexp(n, 100 + b)), numeric(4))
round(rbind(truth = c(r_hi, r_hd, sh, sc),
            gems = rowMeans(G), simpexp = rowMeans(S),
            `mc se (gems)` = apply(G, 1, sd) / sqrt(B),
            `mc se (simpexp)` = apply(S, 1, sd) / sqrt(B)), 4)
#>                 healthy->ill healthy->dead sojourn shape sojourn scale
#> truth                 0.3500        0.0500        1.6000        6.0000
#> gems                  0.3498        0.0481        1.6109        6.0021
#> simpexp               0.3516        0.0489        1.6122        6.0142
#> mc se (gems)          0.0023        0.0006        0.0130        0.0242
#> mc se (simpexp)       0.0026        0.0005        0.0095        0.0150

Both simulators reproduce the exponential exit rates out of healthy and the Weibull sojourn distribution in ill, within Monte-Carlo error.

Summary

comparison reference agreement
single event, piecewise constant msm::rpexp + exact inversion within MC error
single event, Weibull simsurv (continuous inversion) within MC error, grid refines away the discretisation
competing risks closed form + latent failure times within MC error
multi-state, Markov msm::sim.msm, fitted msm model within MC error
multi-state, semi-Markov gems within MC error

The internal test suite adds the checks that do not need another package: Kolmogorov-Smirnov tests against the exponential and Weibull distributions, the cause shares against hj/∑khkh_j/\sum_k h_k, and a round trip in which a piecewise exponential model refitted to the simulated data recovers the coefficients that generated it.
